translations.text: Discourse of our holy father Basil the Great on envy
God is good and the giver of goodness to the good; the devil is evil and the worker of all evil.
And just as freedom from envy is proper to the Good One, so envy befits the evil one.
Let us therefore guard ourselves, brothers, against the passion of envy, so that we may not become sharers in the work of the devil and be found condemned along with him.
For if the proud man is handed over to the judgment of the devil, how shall the envious man not receive the torment prepared for the devil?
For no other passion worse than envy springs up in the souls of men, a passion that does little harm to those outside but is first of all the very own evil of the one who possesses it.
For as rust consumes iron, so envy consumes the soul in which it dwells.
And what is more, just as they say of vipers that they eat through the wombs of their mothers and so come out, so envy consumes the soul that conceives it.
For envy is grief over the good things of one's neighbor; for this reason the envious man is never without grief and distress.
When his neighbor's field abounds with fruit, when his house is in comfort, when that man lacks no joy,
all this becomes an aggravation of the disease and an increase of the wound of the envious man.
And he differs in no way from a naked man whom everyone strikes with arrows.
If someone is brave or prosperous, the envious man is wounded because of it. Is another's face cheerful? Behold, another wound for the envious man.
Does someone surpass many in virtue of soul? Is he praised for wisdom and eloquence?
Is another rich and thriving in acts of mercy to the poor, and is his praise great from those who have received mercy?
All these are wounds and diseases of the envious man, which split his heart open.
And the evil of it is that he cannot even speak of it, but he is bowed down, sorrowful, disheartened and distressed, and he perishes by that evil.
And if anyone asks him, he is ashamed to reveal that affliction and to say:

"I am envious and wicked, and the good things of my friend distress me, and I lament over the joy of my brother, and I cannot bear to see the good things of others, but I regard my neighbor's prosperity as a calamity."
For if he wished to speak the truth, this is what he would say, he who cannot bear to say even one of these things,
but holds that disease in the depths of his soul, where it consumes and devours his insides.
And he accepts neither a physician to heal this disease nor a medicine that might wipe away that passion, although the Scriptures are full of remedies for this disease.
Instead he awaits only one end to that evil: that he may somewhere see fallen those whom he envied.
This is the limit of his hatred: that he may see the one he envied pitiable instead of blessed, and in utter wretchedness.
Only then does he relent and become a friend, when he sees him weeping and mourning.
And when the other rejoiced, he did not rejoice with him, but in the time of weeping he weeps and laments the change in his life, from what state to what state he has changed.
It is not out of love for humanity and mercy that he wipes away his former envy, but so as to make the other's heart ache all the more over his misfortune.
He praises a child after his death and honors him with countless eulogies,
saying how handsome he was to look at, how good a learner, and how skilled in everything, though while the child was in this life he would not have said a kind word to him.
But if he sees many others joining in that praise, he changes again and envies the dead.

In the same way he praises his neighbor's wealth after its collapse, and marvels at his beauty and strength after he has been wasted by illness. Thus he is an enemy of those who are present and a friend of those who are gone.
What then could be worse than this disease? It is the corruption of life, the wound of nature, hatred of what God has granted us, opposition to God.
What brought the source of evils, the devil, to make war on humankind?
Was it not envy, on account of which he is plainly called a fighter against God, for he was hostile to God because of the generous gifts he bestowed on man?
And he did harm to man, since he had no power against what is God's.
And again, Cain too showed himself a doer of the same, that first disciple of the devil, who learned from him both envy and murder, these sibling iniquities,
which the great Paul also joined together when he said: "Full of envy and murder." See, then, what he did?

He saw the honor given by God and was consumed with envy, and he killed the one who was honored, in order to take revenge on the one who gave the honor. For since it was impossible to fight against God, he fell into the killing of his brother.
Let us flee, brothers, from this disease that teaches fighting against God: the mother of murder, the confusion of nature, the ignorance of kinship, this brutish affliction.
Why are you grieved, man, when nothing bad has happened to you? Why do you fight against the one who is prospering, who has taken nothing of yours?
And if he even does you good and still you envy him, are you not envying your own benefit?
What sort of man was Saul, who made the very abundance of benefits a reason for making war on David?
For first, when he was delivered from the evil spirit by that sweet-voiced and divine song, he wished to run his benefactor through with a spear; and then,
when he and his soldiers were delivered by him from their enemies and he was freed from the shame of Goliath,
since in their song of praise the singers assigned ten parts of the victory to David, saying:
"David has slain tens of thousands and Saul thousands," because of this one saying and testimony to the truth he first wished to seize him and kill him secretly, and then he hunted him down.
And even so he did not quiet that enmity, but at last he went out against him with three thousand soldiers, and he roamed through the deserts searching for him.
But if anyone had asked him the reason for his war, would he not have had to name David's great good deeds?
Yet at the time when he was pursuing him, David found him asleep, and he was ready to be killed by that enemy of his, but he was spared once again,
when the righteous man was unwilling to lay hands on him. And even by this good deed he was not swayed, but again sought him out and pursued him,
until he was found by David a second time, in a cave, and David made his own virtue more brilliant still and the other's wickedness manifest.
Envy is a hostility hard to reconcile, for with other kinds of enemies good deeds soften them, but every good thing inflames the envious man all the more;
and the more greatly one honors him, the more he envies and the more resentful and aggrieved he is, for he envies his benefactor more than he is grateful to him.
What beast do such people not surpass in wickedness? What savage do they not exceed in savagery?
Dogs are calmed by feeding, lions are tamed by habit, but the envious are made all the fiercer by good things.
What enslaved that valiant Joseph? Was it not the envy of his brothers? The sickness of their envy is indeed worthy of wonder,
for they feared the fulfillment of the dreams and therefore gave their brother into slavery, so that it might never be possible for a slave to be bowed down to.
But tell me, you: if the dream is true, what means could there be to keep what was foretold from being fulfilled?
And if it is false, why then do you envy a man who is deluded? But as it was, by the providence of God their cleverness was overturned:
for by the very deeds through which they thought to destroy his being bowed down to, by these they proved rather to be the ones leading the way to that outcome.
For if he had not been sold, he would not have gone down to Egypt; he would not, because of his chastity, have been given over to a struggle against the desires of that wicked woman;
he would not have fallen into prison, he would not have become acquainted with those servants of Pharaoh, he would not have made that revelation of the dreams,
through which he received the rule of Egypt, and because of the shortage of wheat his brothers went down there and bowed down to him.
Go on in word to that great envy, committed over great things, which came about through the wickedness of the Jews against Christ the Savior.
For why did they envy him? Because of the miracles. And what were those miracles?
The life of humankind. The hungry were fed, and they envied the one who fed them;
the dead were raised, and those wicked men were hostile to the one who raised them; demons were cast out, and they spoke evil of the one who cast them out;
lepers were cleansed, the lame walked, the deaf heard, the blind saw, and they persecuted that benefactor.
And at last they handed over to death the giver of life, and scourged the liberator of humankind, and condemned the judge of the world.
Thus the evil of envy reached to all things, and with this one weapon, from the beginning of the world, that enemy of our life, the devil, has been striking [?] and wounds and casts down everyone,
he who rejoices at our destruction, who fell through envy and has cast us down along with himself by the same passion.
Wise, then, was the one who commands that no one even eat with an envious man, and by that eating signifies every sharing of life.
For just as we hasten to place easily burned material far from fire,
so it is necessary to flee from association and conversation with the envious, so that we may place ourselves out of reach of those arrows of envy.
For envy comes about in no other way than through kinship, for according to the word of Solomon, a man's envy comes from his neighbor.
For so indeed it is: the Egyptian does not envy the Roman, but each one envies his own people, and among his own people not those who are strangers to him,
but those whom he knows, and among his acquaintances, those who are close to him and his companions and kinsmen, and also those of his own age, and most of all brothers and sisters.
And as blight is wheat's own disease, so envy is the disease of a friend.
This alone is praiseworthy in that evil: the more fiercely it is stirred up, the worse it is for the one who possesses it.
For as arrows traveling swiftly, when they strike some firm and resisting object, turn back upon the one who sent them,
so those stirrings of envy harm nothing in those against whom they are directed, but become a wound to the envious person himself.
For who has ever, by his own distress, diminished the good things of his neighbor? Rather, he harms his own self, punished by that very grief.
And again, the envious are reckoned by some to be even worse than snakes, for they say that
snakes inject their venom by biting, and the one struck rots away little by little, whereas the envious do harm even through their eyes,
so that bodies well-fed and beautiful melt away under the gaze of the envious, and their beauty wastes away,
for venom comes out from the eyes of the envious and, like a river, carries off their beauty, ruins it, and gives it over to decay.
But I reject this saying and hold it unbelievable, as a fable brought in by foolish women.
Rather, I say this: that the demons who hate the good, when they find a mind receptive to them,
then make use of it in every way according to their own will, so that they even use the very eyes of the envious in the service of their will.
Now then, are you not afraid to enter into the slavery of the devil, that wicked and evil one, and to take in that evil,
through which you become an enemy of those from whom you have suffered no harm at all, and an enemy of the good and unenvying God?
Let us flee, brothers, from this unseemly evil. This is the teaching of that serpent, devised by the devil, sown by the enemy,
a pledge of hell and a hindrance to godliness, a road leading to Gehenna, an expeller from the Kingdom.
The envious can be recognized even by their faces: for their eye is dry and lusterless, their cheeks gloomy and wasted,
their brows lowered, their soul disturbed by that passion, and it does not have true judgment concerning matters.
Their conduct is not praiseworthy for virtue, nor is the power of their speech adorned with honor and grace, nor do they have anything else among the things that are to be envied and called blessed.
But as vultures go to carcasses, flying past many fragrant and beautiful places and going to that stench,
and flies pass by the healthy places and go to pus and rotten flesh,
so the envious do not look at all to the splendors of life and the greatness of virtues, but rush to what is base and look at that;
And if they see those whom they envy stumbling somewhere in some matter, as stumbling happens among people, they publicize it and want that man's name to be known by it.
Like those crafty painters who, from the crookedness of a nose, or of some other limb, or from a wound,
whether it exists by nature or has befallen him, learn from it the likenesses of those they portray, so are these evil men.
By turning toward what is base, they cast aside what is praiseworthy and accuse virtue by means of the vice that lies next to it: for they call the brave man arrogant and the calm man unmerciful,
the just man merciless and the wise man wicked, and they accuse the very magnificent man as vain, the generous man as prodigal, and the good manager as mean.
And in this way there is no form of virtue that they cannot turn into the opposite vice. What then?
Shall we end our discourse with this reproach and accusation of evil? But this is only about half of the cure.
For it is not useless to show the sick man the greatness of his disease, so that he may take due care over it;
but to leave the sick man at this point and not tell him in what way he may come to health is utterly improper.
What then shall I say: how may we avoid falling into that disease from the first, or, if we have fallen into it, how may we escape?
First, then, let nothing among human affairs be reckoned great by us: neither the wealth of the world, nor that passing glory,
nor the beauty of the body. For the limit of the good does not lie in these passing things, but we are called to those eternal good things.
For the rich man is not to be envied for his wealth, nor the glorious man for the abundance of his honor, nor the strong man for the power of his flesh,
nor the wise man for his eloquence. For all these are instruments of virtue for those who use them well, and they do not hold blessedness in themselves.
For whoever uses them badly is pitiable, like one who willingly kills himself with the sword he has received for fighting enemies.
But if someone uses them well and fittingly, and is a steward of the things of God, and does not store them up for his own ease,
such a man is justly to be praised and loved for his love of the brethren and his sharing with others.
Again, if someone is lofty in wisdom, honored by the word of God, and an interpreter of the divine words, do not envy such a man,
nor ever wish that the speaker of those holy words should fall silent, if by the grace of God his hearers find acceptance and benefit.
For that good is yours, and the gift of teaching is granted to you through that brother, if you are willing to accept it.
For no one stops up a gushing spring, and when the sun is shining no one shuts his eyes or envies them, but rather prays for himself that he may always be a receiver of them.
But when a spiritual word springs up in the church and comes forth from a pure heart by the grace of the Holy Spirit, will you not hold out your ears with joy?
Will you not accept that benefit with thanks?
But what pains you is the praise of those present, who were praising the speaker; or else you would wish that no one had benefited and that no one had praised him.
What word will anyone have to say about this before the Judge of our hearts, since by nature it is right to call virtue and spiritual goodness good?
But as for one who excels in wealth and prides himself on power and on bodily beauty, if he uses well what he has,
he ought to be loved, as one who holds a common instrument of this life for everyone, when he uses it well and is ungrudging with his goods toward all
who are in need, and with his own body serves the weak well, and reckons all his possessions as belonging no more to himself than to the poor.
But one who is not like this in these matters ought rather to be pitied and not envied,
for he has greater occasions for evil, since this is destruction with abundant preparation.
For if wealth becomes for him a provision for destruction, that rich man is to be pitied and not envied;
but if that wealth is a helper of virtue, envy no longer has any place there, since its benefit is common to all,
unless someone, through that abundance of wickedness, should begrudge even himself these good things.
And in sum, if in your mind you rise above human affairs and look to what is truly good and praiseworthy,
what could then persuade you to reckon any of those corruptible and earthly things as blessed and enviable?
But when you are thus, and the affairs of this world do not seem wondrous to you, as though they were some great glories, it is impossible that envy should ever master you.
But if you are eager for glory and wish to be above the many, and for this reason do not endure being inferior (for this thought too is a great cause of envy),
listen to me, and I will show you the glory that you should desire: turn that love of honor of yours toward the acquisition of virtues,
for do not desire earthly glory and worldly wealth, because this is not within your power.
But be righteous, holy and wise, courageous and patient in the contests of piety.
For in this way you will both save yourself and gain an even higher glory upon those higher goods.
For virtue is within our power, and its acquisition is possible for everyone who is diligent,
but wealth and bodily beauty and strength and human glory are not within our power.
Now, if virtue is both the highest good and firm, and its honor is acknowledged by all, let us pursue it,
the acquisition of which is impossible for a soul that is not pure of the other passions and, above all, of all envy.
Do you not see how evil double-mindedness is? It too is a fruit of envy, for duplicity of manner arises among people from envy more than from anything else,
when they hold hatred in the depths of the soul and display an outward appearance dyed with love,
like those hidden rocks in the sea, which are covered by a little water and, unseen, become a snare to the unwary.
Let us understand, then, how from this passion death sprang up upon us, as from a spring,
the fall from good things, estrangement from God, disobedience to the commandments, and the corruption of every good thing.
And let us learn the word of the Apostle, that "we should not be arrogant, provoking one another, envying one another,"
but rather "gentle, kind, forgiving one another, just as God has forgiven us through Christ Jesus
our Lord," to whom belong glory and might, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and unto the ages of ages, amen.
